entries.e0c530bb4a7a49bc9959dd2e3f41ea83065a65a5: <div sID="gen15992" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Isa.25" sID="Isa.25"/> <div eID="gen15992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15993" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15994" type="x-p"/> After the threatenings of wrath in the foregoing chapter we have here, I. Thankful praises for what God had done, which the prophet, in the name of the church, offers up to God, and teaches us to offer the like, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Precious promises of what God would yet further do for his church, especially in the grace of the gospel, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6-Isa.25.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. The church's triumph in God over her enemies thereupon, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9-Isa.25.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. This chapter looks as pleasantly upon the church as the former looked dreadfully upon the world.
entries.a6ad9abb04021c8e2d2c7cbdfc8f29d24ba13a64: <div eID="gen15994" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15993" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Song of Praise. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful <hi type="italic">things; thy</hi> counsels of old <hi type="italic">are</hi> faithfulness <hi type="italic">and</hi> truth. <hi type="super">2</hi> For thou hast made of a city a heap; <hi type="italic">of</hi> a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a storm <hi type="italic">against</hi> the wall. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place; <hi type="italic">even</hi> the heat with the shadow of a cloud: the branch of the terrible ones shall be brought low. <div eID="gen15995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15996" type="x-p"/> It is said in the close of the foregoing chapter that the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts shall reign gloriously;</hi> now, in compliance with this, the prophet here speaks of <hi type="italic">the glorious majesty of his kingdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.12">Ps. cxlv. 12</reference>), and gives him the glory of it; and, however this prophecy might have an accomplishment in the destruction of Babylon and the deliverance of the Jews out of their captivity there, it seems to look further, to the praises that should be offered up to God by the gospel church for Christ's victories over our spiritual enemies and the comforts he has provided for all believers. Here, <div eID="gen15996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15997" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet determines to praise God himself; for those that would stir up others should in the first place stir up themselves to praise God (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! thou art my God,</hi> a God in covenant with me." When God is punishing <hi type="italic">the kings of the earth upon the earth,</hi> and making them to tremble before him, a poor prophet can go to him, and, with a humble boldness, say, <hi type="italic">O Lord! thou art my God,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name.</hi> Those that have the Lord for their God are bound to praise him; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he took us to be his people <hi type="italic">that we might be unto him for a name and for a praise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>. In praising God we exalt him; not that we can make him higher than he is, but we must make him to appear to ourselves and others than he does. See <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exod. xv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen15997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15998" type="x-p"/> II. He pleases himself with the thought that others also shall be brought to praise God, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.3">v. 3</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because of the <hi type="italic">desolations thou hast made in the earth</hi> by thy providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.8">Ps. xlvi. 8</reference>) and the just vengeance thou hast taken on thy and thy church's enemies, <hi type="italic">therefore shall the strong people glorify thee</hi> in concert, <hi type="italic">and the city</hi> (the metropolis) <hi type="italic">of the terrible nations fear thee.</hi>" This may be understood, 1. Of those people that have been strong and terrible against God. Those that have been enemies to God's kingdom, and have fought against the interests of it with a great deal of strength and terror, shall either be converted, and glorify God by joining with his people in his service, or at least convinced, so as to own themselves conquered. Those that have been the terror of the mighty shall be forced to tremble before the judgments of God and call in vain to rocks and mountains to hide them. Or, 2. Of those that shall be now made strong and terrible for God and by him, though before they were weak and trampled upon. God shall so visibly appear for and with those that fear him and glorify him that all shall acknowledge them a strong people and shall stand in awe of them. There was a time when <hi type="italic">many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Esther viii. 17</reference>), and when those that knew their God were strong and did exploits (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">Dan. xi. 32</reference>), for which they glorified God. <div eID="gen15998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15999" type="x-p"/> III. He observes what is, and ought to be, the matter of this praise. We and others must exalt God and praise him; for, 1. He has done wonders, according to the counsel of his own will, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1">v. 1</reference>. We exalt God by admiring what he has done as truly wonderful, wonderful proofs of his power beyond what any creature could perform, and wonderful proofs of his goodness beyond what such sinful creatures as we are could expect. These <hi type="italic">wonderful things,</hi> which are new and surprising to us, and altogether unthought of, are according to his <hi type="italic">counsels of old,</hi> devised by his wisdom and designed for his own glory and the comfort of his people. All the operations of providence are according to God's eternal counsels (and those faithfulness and truth itself), all consonant to his attributes, consistent with one another, and sure to be accomplished in their season. 2. He has in particular humbled the pride, and broken the power, of the mighty ones of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast made of a city,</hi> of many a city, <hi type="italic">a heap</hi> of rubbish. Of many a defenced city, that thought itself well guarded by nature and art, and the multitude and courage of its militia, thou hast made a ruin." What created strength can hold out against Omnipotence? "Many a city so richly built that it might be called a <hi type="italic">palace,</hi> and so much frequented and visited by persons of the best rank from all parts that it might be called a <hi type="italic">palace of strangers,</hi> thou hast made to be no city; it is levelled with the ground, and not one stone left upon another, and it shall never be built again." This has been the case of many cities in divers parts of the world, and in our own nation particularly; cities that flourished once have gone to decay and are lost, and it is scarcely known (except by urns or coins digged up out of the earth) where they stood. How many of the cities of Israel have long since been heaps and ruins! God hereby teaches us that <hi type="italic">here we have no continuing city</hi> and must therefore seek one to come which will never be a ruin or go to decay. 3. He has seasonably relieved and succoured his necessitous and distressed people (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou has been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy.</hi> As God weakens the strong that are proud and secure, so he strengthens the weak that are humble and serious, and stay themselves upon him. Nay, he not only makes them strong, but he is himself their strength; for in him they strengthen themselves, and it is his favour that is the <hi type="italic">strength of their hearts.</hi> He is a <hi type="italic">strength to the needy in his distress,</hi> when he needs strength, and when his distress drives him to God. And, as he strengthens them against their inward decays, so he shelters them from outward assaults. He is <hi type="italic">a refuge from the storm</hi> of rain or hail, and <hi type="italic">a shadow from the</hi> scorching <hi type="italic">heat</hi> of the sun in summer. God is a sufficient protection to his people in all weathers, hot and cold, wet and dry. The armour of righteousness serves both <hi type="italic">on the right hand</hi> and <hi type="italic">on the left,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2 Cor. vi. 7</reference>. Whatever dangers or troubles God's people may be in, effectual care is taken that they shall sustain no real hurt or damage. When perils are most threatening and alarming God will then appear for the safety of his people: <hi type="italic">When the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall,</hi> which makes a great noise, but cannot overthrow the wall. The enemies of God's poor are terrible ones; they do all they can to make themselves so to them. Their rage is like a blast of wind, loud, and blustering, and furious; but, like the wind, it is under a divine check; for God <hi type="italic">holds the winds in his fist,</hi> and God will be such a shelter to his people that they shall be able to stand the shock, keep their ground, and maintain their integrity and peace. A storm beating on a ship tosses it, but that which beats on a wall never stirs it, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Ps. lxxvi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.7">cxxxviii. 7</reference>. 4. That he does and will shelter those that trust in him from the insolence of their proud oppressors (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt,</hi> or thou dost, <hi type="italic">bring down the noise of strangers;</hi> thou shalt abate and still it, as <hi type="italic">the heat in a dry place</hi> is abated and moderated <hi type="italic">by the shadow of a cloud</hi> interposing. <hi type="italic">The branch,</hi> or rather the son or triumph, <hi type="italic">of the terrible ones shall be brought low,</hi> and they shall be made to change their note and lower their voice. Observe here, (1.) The oppressors of God's people are called <hi type="italic">strangers;</hi> for they forget that those they oppress are made of the same mould, of the same blood, with them. They are called <hi type="italic">terrible ones;</hi> for so they affect to be, rather than amiable ones: they would rather be feared than loved. (2.) Their insolence towards the people of God is noisy and hot, and that is all; it is but the noise of strangers, who think to carry their point by hectoring and bullying all that stand in their way, and talking big. <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.46.17">Jer. xlvi. 17</reference>. It is like the heat of the sun scorching in the middle of the day; but where is it when the sun has set? (3.) Their noise, and heat, and all their triumph, will be humbled and brought low, when their hopes are baffled and all their honours laid in the dust. The branches, even the top branches, of the terrible ones, will be broken off, and thrown to the dunghill. (4.) If the labourers in God's vineyard be at any time called to <hi type="italic">bear the burden and heat of the day,</hi> he will find some way or other to refresh them, as with the shadow of a cloud, that they may not be pressed above measure.
entries.eb10ad3f1d47d45e2edc2291705cbfaf0bebdcfd: <div eID="gen15999" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blessings of the Gospel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen16000" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And in this mountain shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations. <hi type="super">8</hi> He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen16000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16001" type="x-p"/> If we suppose (as many do) that this refers to the great joy which there should be in Zion and Jerusalem when the army of the Assyrians was routed by an angel, or when the Jews were released out of their captivity in Babylon, or upon occasion of some other equally surprising deliverance, yet we cannot avoid making it to look further, to the grace of the gospel and the glory which is the crown and consummation of that grace; for it is at our resurrection through Christ that the saying here written <hi type="italic">shall be brought to pass;</hi> then, and not till then (if we may believe St. Paul), it shall have its full accomplishment: <hi type="italic">Death is swallowed up in victory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">1 Cor. xv. 54</reference>. This is a key to the rest of the promises here connected together. And so we have here a prophecy of the salvation and the grace brought unto us by Jesus Christ, into which <hi type="italic">the prophets enquired and searched diligently,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1 Pet. i. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen16001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16002" type="x-p"/> I. That the grace of the gospel should be a royal feast for all people; not like that of Ahasuerus, which was intended only to show the grandeur of the master of the feast (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.4">Esther i. 4</reference>); for this is intended to gratify the guests, and therefore, whereas all <hi type="italic">there</hi> was for show, all <hi type="italic">here</hi> is for substance. The preparations made in the gospel for the kind reception of penitents and supplicants with God are often in the New Testament set forth by the similitude of <hi type="italic">a feast,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Matt.22.1">Matt. xxii. 1</reference>, &c., which seems to be borrowed from this prophecy. 1. God himself is the Master of the feast, and we may be sure he prepares like himself, as becomes him to give, rather than as becomes us to receive. <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts</hi> makes this feast. 2. The guests invited are <hi type="italic">all people,</hi> Gentiles as well as Jews. <hi type="italic">Go preach the gospel to every creature.</hi> There is enough for all, and whoever will may come, and partake freely, even those that are gathered out of the highways and the hedges. 3. The place is <hi type="italic">Mount Zion.</hi> Thence the preaching of the gospel takes rise: the preachers must begin at Jerusalem. The gospel church is the Jerusalem that is above; there this feast is made, and to it all the invited guests must go. 4. The provision is very rich, and every thing is of the best. It is a <hi type="italic">feast,</hi> which supposes abundance and variety; it is a continual feast to believers, it is their own fault if it be not. It is <hi type="italic">a feast of fat things and full of marrow;</hi> so relishing, so nourishing, are the comforts of the gospel to all those that feast upon them and digest them. The returning prodigal was entertained with the fatted calf; and David has that pleasure in communion with God with which his soul is satisfied as with marrow and fatness. It is a feast <hi type="italic">of wines on the lees,</hi> the strongest-bodied wines, that have been kept long upon the lees, and then are well refined from them, so that they are clear and fine. There is that in the gospel which, like wine soberly used, makes glad the heart and raises the spirits, and is fit for those that are of a heavy heart, being under convictions of sin and mourning for it, that they may drink and forget their misery (for that is the proper use of wine—it is a cordial for those that need it, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5-Prov.31.6">Prov. xxxi. 5, 6</reference>), may be of good cheer, knowing that their sins are forgiven, and may be vigorous in their spiritual work and warfare, as a strong man refreshed with wine. <div eID="gen16002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16003" type="x-p"/> II. That the world should be freed from that darkness of ignorance and mistake in the mists of which it had been so long lost and buried (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering</hi> (the covering of the face) with which all people are covered (hood-winked or blind-folded) so that they cannot see their way nor go about their work, and by reason of which they wander endlessly. Their faces are covered as those of men condemned, or dead men. There is <hi type="italic">a veil spread over all nations,</hi> for they all sit in darkness; and no marvel, when the Jews themselves, among whom <hi type="italic">God was known,</hi> had a <hi type="italic">veil upon their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">2 Cor. iii. 15</reference>. But this veil the Lord will destroy, by the light of his gospel shining in the world, and the power of his Spirit opening men's eyes to receive it. He will raise those to spiritual life that have long been dead in trespasses and sins. <div eID="gen16003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16004" type="x-p"/> III. That death should be conquered, the power of it broken, and the property of it altered: <hi type="italic">He will swallow up death in victory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">v. 8</reference>. 1. Christ will himself, in his resurrection, triumph over death, will break its bands, its bars, asunder, and cast away all its cords. The grave seemed to swallow him up, but really he swallowed it up. 2. The happiness of the saints shall be out of the reach of death, which puts a period to all the enjoyments of this world, embitters them, and stains the beauty of them. 3. Believers may triumph over death, and look upon it as a conquered enemy: <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> 4. When the dead bodies of the saints shall be raised at the great day, and their mortality swallowed up of life, then death will be for ever swallowed up of victory; and it is the last enemy. <div eID="gen16004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16005" type="x-p"/> IV. That grief shall be banished, and there shall be perfect and endless joy: <hi type="italic">The Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces.</hi> Those that mourn for sin shall be comforted and have their consciences pacified. In the covenant of grace there shall be that provided which is sufficient to counterbalance all the sorrows of this present time, to wipe away our tears, and to refresh us. Those particularly that suffer for Christ shall have consolations abounding as their afflictions do abound. But in the joys of heaven, and nowhere short of them, will fully be <hi type="italic">brought to pass this saying,</hi> as that before, for there it is that God shall <hi type="italic">wipe away all tears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.17">Rev. vii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">xxi. 4</reference>. And <hi type="italic">there shall be no more sorrow,</hi> because <hi type="italic">there shall be no more death.</hi> The hope of this should now wipe away all excessive tears, all the weeping that hinders sowing. <div eID="gen16005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16006" type="x-p"/> V. That all the reproach cast upon religion and the serious professors of it shall be for ever rolled away: <hi type="italic">The rebuke of his people,</hi> which they have long lain under, the calumnies and misrepresentations by which they have been blackened, the insolence and cruelty with which their persecutors have trampled on them and trodden them down, <hi type="italic">shall be taken away.</hi> Their righteousness shall be brought forth as the light, in the view of all the world, who shall be convinced that they are not such as they have been invidiously characterized; and so their salvation from the injuries done them as such shall be wrought out. Sometimes in this world God does that for his people which <hi type="italic">takes away their reproach from among men.</hi> However, it will be done effectually at the great day; for the <hi type="italic">Lord has spoken it,</hi> who can, and will, make it good. Let us patiently bear sorrow and shame now, and improve both; for shortly both will be done away.
entries.f0dac9ced128f503cd50ccc4aa6dfa8d0f099971: <div eID="gen16006" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blessings of the Gospel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen16007" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation. <hi type="super">10</hi> For in this mountain shall the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rest, and Moab shall be trodden down under him, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth <hi type="italic">his hands</hi> to swim: and he shall bring down their pride together with the spoils of their hands. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bring to the ground, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the dust. <div eID="gen16007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16008" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The welcome which the church shall give to these blessings promised in the foregoing verses (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">It shall be said in that day,</hi> with a humble holy triumph and exultation, <hi type="italic">Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him!</hi> Thus will the deliverance of the church out of long and sore troubles be celebrated; thus will it be as life from the dead. With such transports of joy and praise will those entertain the glad tidings of the Redeemer who looked for him, and for redemption in Jerusalem by him; and with such a triumphant song as this will glorified saints <hi type="italic">enter into the joy of their Lord.</hi> 1. God himself must have the glory of all: "<hi type="italic">Lo, this is our God, this is the Lord.</hi> This which is done is his doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes. Herein he has done like himself, has magnified his own wisdom, power, and goodness. Herein he has done for us like our God, a God in covenant with us, and whom we serve." Note, Our triumphs must not terminate in what God does for us and gives to us, but must pass through them to himself, who is the author and giver of them: <hi type="italic">This is our God.</hi> Have any of the nations of the earth such a God to trust to? No, <hi type="italic">their rock is not as our rock. There is none like unto the God of Jerusalem.</hi> 2. The longer it has been expected the more welcome it is. "This is he whom we have waited for, in dependence upon his word of promise, and a full assurance that he would come in the set time, in due time, and therefore we were willing to tarry his time; and now we find it is not in vain to wait for him, for the mercy comes at last, with an abundant recompence for the delay." 3. It is matter of joy unspeakable: "<hi type="italic">We will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.</hi> We that share in the benefits of it will concur in the joyful thanksgivings for it." 4. It is an encouragement to hope for the continuance and perfection of this salvation: <hi type="italic">We have waited for him, and he will save us,</hi> will carry on what he has begun; for <hi type="italic">as for God,</hi> our God, <hi type="italic">his work is perfect.</hi> <div eID="gen16008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16009" type="x-p"/> II. A prospect of further blessings for the securing and perpetuating of these. 1. The power of God shall be engaged for them and shall continue to take their part: <hi type="italic">In this mountain shall the hand of the Lord rest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.10">v. 10</reference>. The church and people of God shall have continued proofs of God's presence with them and residence among them: his hand shall be continually over them, to protect and guard them, and continually stretched out to them, for their supply. Mount Zion is <hi type="italic">his rest for ever;</hi> here he will dwell. 2. The power of their enemies, which is engaged against them, shall be broken. <hi type="italic">Moab</hi> is here put for all the adversaries of God's people, that are vexatious to them; they <hi type="italic">shall</hi> all <hi type="italic">be trodden down</hi> or threshed (for <hi type="italic">then</hi> they beat out the corn by treading it) and shall be thrown out as <hi type="italic">straw to the dunghill,</hi> being good for nothing else. God having <hi type="italic">caused his hand to rest upon this mountain,</hi> it shall not be a hand that hangs down, or is folded up, feeble and inactive; but he shall <hi type="italic">spread forth his hands, in the midst</hi> of his people, <hi type="italic">like one that swims,</hi> which intimates that he will employ and exert his power for them vigorously,—that he will be doing for them on all sides,—that he will easily and effectually put by the opposition that is given to his gracious intentions for them, and thereby further and push forward his good work among them,—and that on their behalf he will be continually active, for so the swimmer is. It is foretold, particularly, what he shall do for them. (1.) <hi type="italic">He shall bring down the pride</hi> of their enemies (and Moab was notoriously guilty of pride, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">ch. xvi. 6</reference>) by one humbling judgment after another, stripping them of that which they are proud of. (2.) He shall bring down <hi type="italic">the spoils of their hands,</hi> shall take from them that which they have got by spoil and rapine. He shall bring down the arms of their hands, which are lifted up against God's Israel; he shall quite break their power, and disable them to do mischief. (3.) He shall ruin all their fortifications, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.12">v. 12</reference>. Moab has his walls, and his high forts, with which he hopes to secure himself, and from which he designs to annoy the people of God; but God shall <hi type="italic">bring them all down, lay them low, bring them to the ground, to the dust;</hi> and so those who trusted to them will be left exposed. There is no fortress impregnable to Omnipotence, no fort so high but the arm of the Lord can overtop it and bring it down. This destruction of Moab is typical of Christ's victory over death (spoken of <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">v. 8</reference>), his spoiling principalities and powers in his cross (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>), his pulling down Satan's strong-holds by the preaching of his gospel (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2 Cor. x. 4</reference>), and his reigning till all his enemies be <hi type="italic">made his footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>.  <chapter eID="Isa.25"/> <div eID="gen16009" type="x-p"/>

entries.29b4c492b96b511ad0b0a65df3cd6fcdfbc95d13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8757"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.12">Is 25:1-12</reference>. Continuation of the Twenty-fourth Chapter. Thanksgiving for the Overthrow of the Apostate Faction, and the Setting Up of Jehovah's Throne on Zion.</title> <div sID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> The restoration from Babylon and re-establishment of the theocracy was a type and pledge of this.<div eID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8757"/><hi type="bold">1. wonderful--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsels of old--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.42.9">Is 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">46:10</reference>). Purposes planned long ago; here, as to the deliverance of His people.<div eID="gen14524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth--</hi>Hebrew, Amen; covenant-keeping, faithful to promises; the peculiar characteristic of Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.14">Re 3:14</reference>). <div eID="gen14525" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ec4a9f736652f38b9ac0a58b1ac708265fbdac1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8758"/><div sID="gen14526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8758"/><hi type="bold">2. a city ... heap--</hi>Babylon, type of the seat of Antichrist, to be destroyed in the last days (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.37">Jr 51:37</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Rev.18.1-Rev.18.24">Re 18:1-24</reference>, followed, as here, by the song of the saints' thanksgiving in <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.21">Re 19:1-21</reference>). "Heaps" is a graphic picture of Babylon and Nineveh as they now are.<div eID="gen14526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">palace--</hi>Babylon regarded, on account of its splendor, as a vast palace. But Maurer translates, "a citadel."<div eID="gen14527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of strangers--</hi>foreigners, whose capital pre-eminently Babylon was, the metropolis of the pagan world. "Aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise" (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">Is 29:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>; see in contrast, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.17">Joe 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen14528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">never be built--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Is 13:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">20</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen14529" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca75739066e32e5aa797ddc7eefb20ab126c749b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8759"/><div sID="gen14530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8759"/><hi type="bold">3. strong people--</hi>This cannot apply to the Jews; but other nations on which Babylon had exercised its cruelty (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.12">Is 14:12</reference>) shall worship Jehovah, awed by the judgment inflicted on Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Is 23:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">city--</hi>not Babylon, which shall then be destroyed, but collectively for the cities of the surrounding nations. <div eID="gen14531" type="x-p"/>
entries.383ba9929cbaaf045b006691df69196fec29ed24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8760"/><div sID="gen14532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8760"/><hi type="bold">4. the poor ... needy--</hi>the Jews, exiles from their country (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.6">Is 26:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.17">41:17</reference>).<div eID="gen14532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heat--</hi>calamity (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">32:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blast--</hi>that is, wrath.<div eID="gen14534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">storm--</hi>a tempest of rain, a winter flood, rushing against and overthrowing the wall of a house. <div eID="gen14535" type="x-p"/>
entries.10fb1b6ccbb63a6e5974d850221f9796f54ced5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8761"/><div sID="gen14536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8761"/>5. Translate, "As the heat in a dry land (is brought down by the shadow of a cloud, so) thou shalt bring down the tumult (the shout of triumph over their enemies) of strangers (foreigners); and as the heat by the shadow of the cloud (is brought low), so the branch (the offspring) of the terrible ones shall be brought low." Parkhurst translates the Hebrew for "branch," the exulting song. Jerome translates the last clause, "And as when the heat burns under a cloud, thou shalt make the branch of the terrible ones to wither"; the branch withering even under the friendly shade of a cloud typifies the wicked brought to ruin, not for want of natural means of prosperity, but by the immediate act of God. <div eID="gen14536" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b79bc8a39ed83b1508598982f6639924dd51971: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8762"/><div sID="gen14537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8762"/><hi type="bold">6. in this mountain--</hi>Zion: Messiah's kingdom was to begin, and is to have its central seat hereafter, at Jerusalem, as the common country of "all nations" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen14537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all people--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Is 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.10">Lu 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feast--</hi>image of felicity (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Psa 22:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">Mt 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.15">Lu 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">Re 19:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.1-Ps.87.7">87:1-7</reference>).<div eID="gen14539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fat things--</hi>delicacies; the rich mercies of God in Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.14">Jr 31:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>).<div eID="gen14540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wines on the lees--</hi>wine which has been long kept on the lees; that is, the oldest and most generous wine (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jr 48:11</reference>).<div eID="gen14541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">marrow--</hi>the choicest dainties (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">well refined--</hi>cleared of all dregs. <div eID="gen14543" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd7d5a2b944a31f9793f7af91785a4009d829953: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8763"/><div sID="gen14544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8763"/><hi type="bold">7. face of ... covering--</hi>image from mourning, in which it was usual to cover the face with a veil (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). "Face of covering," that is, the covering itself; as in <reference osisRef="Job.41.13">Job 41:13</reference>, "the face of his garment," the garment itself. The covering or veil is the mist of ignorance as to a future state, and the way to eternal life, which enveloped the nations (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>) and the unbelieving Jew (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">2Co 3:15</reference>). The Jew, however, is first to be converted before the conversion of "all nations"; for it is "in this mountain," namely, Zion, that the latter are to have the veil taken off (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.13">Psa 102:13</reference>, 15, 16, 21, 22; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14544" type="x-p"/>
entries.63fbdc7506a6a2acac1a6b5d125314bf1a39346a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8764"/><div sID="gen14545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8764"/>8. Quoted in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">1Co 15:54</reference>, in support of the resurrection.<div eID="gen14545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swallow up ... in victory--</hi>completely and permanently "abolish" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">Re 20:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">21:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.17">Ge 2:17</reference>; 3:22).<div eID="gen14546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rebuke--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Mark.8.38">Mr 8:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>). <div eID="gen14547" type="x-p"/>
entries.77b8886a3471ac44189ec4bc23434b00c569c71d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8765"/><div sID="gen14548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8765"/><hi type="bold">9. And it shall be said in that day, &c.--</hi>"After death has been swallowed up for ever, the people of God, who had been delivered from the hand of death, shall say to the Lord, Lo, this is our God, whom unbelievers regarded as only a man" [Jerome]. "The words are so moulded as to point us specially to the person of the Son of God, who 'saves' us; as He vouchsafed to Israel temporal saving, so to His elect He appears for the purpose of conferring eternal salvation" [Vitringa]. The Jews, however, have a special share in the words, This is our God (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Is 25:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have waited--</hi>"Waited" is characteristic of God's people in all ages (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.18">Ge 49:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen14549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation--</hi>compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.24">Psa 118:24</reference>, which refers to the second coming of Jesus (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">Psa 118:26</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Luke.13.35">Lu 13:35</reference>). <div eID="gen14550" type="x-p"/>
entries.51ed56ae6b52a71e4ab33ac8cea3a3b7f6966957: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8766"/><div sID="gen14551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8766"/><hi type="bold">10. rest--</hi>as its permanent protector; on "hand" in this sense; compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.6">Ezr 7:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.28">28</reference>.<div eID="gen14551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Moab--</hi>while Israel is being protected, the foe is destroyed; Moab is the representative of all the foes of God's people.<div eID="gen14552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under him--</hi>Rather, "in his own place" or "country" (<reference osisRef="Exod.10.23">Ex 10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.16.29">16:29</reference>).<div eID="gen14553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the dunghill--</hi>Rather, "in the water of the dung heap," in which straw was trodden to make it manure (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>). Horsley translates either, "in the waters of Madmenah," namely, for the making of bricks; or as the Septuagint, "as the threshing-floor is trampled by the corn-drag" (see Margin; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.13">Mi 4:11-13</reference>). <div eID="gen14554" type="x-p"/>
entries.05b014212be28fe8337fbe3d8150e98c8aa6a4c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8767"/><div sID="gen14555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8767"/><hi type="bold">11. he--</hi>Jehovah shall spread His hands to strike the foe on this side and on that, with as little effort as a swimmer spreads forth his arms to cleave a passage through the water [Calvin]. (<reference osisRef="Zech.5.3">Zec 5:3</reference>). Lowth takes "he" as Moab, who, in danger of sinking, shall strain every nerve to save himself; but Jehovah (and "he") shall cause him to sink ("bring down the pride" of Moab, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the spoils of ... hands--</hi>literally, "the craftily acquired spoils" of his (Moab's) hands [Barnes]. Moab's pride, as well as the sudden gripe of his hands (namely, whereby he tries to save himself from drowning) [Lowth]. "Together with the joints of his hands," that is, though Moab struggle against Jehovah hand and foot [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14556" type="x-p"/>
entries.f18447c23b9a61e57c1038baf917fdf25336bd9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8768"/><div sID="gen14557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8768"/><hi type="bold">12. fortress--</hi>the strongholds of Moab, the representative of the foes of God's people [Barnes]. Babylon [Maurer]. The society of infidels represented as a city (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.25"/>

entries.6e5dedb511431edf9c6e9db5317dc38377e496a5: <div eID="gen27489" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27490" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27491" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27491" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27490" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27492" type="x-p"/> The short glance which the prophet gave at the promised restoration of the people of God and the Messiah's kingdom, in the close of the preceding chapter, makes him break out into a rapturous song of praise in this, where although he alludes to temporal mercies, such as the destruction of the cities which had been at war with Zion, the ruin of Moab, and other signal interpositions of Divine Providence in behalf of the Jews; yet he is evidently impressed with a more lively sense of future and much higher blessings under the Gospel dispensation, in the plenitude of its revelation, of which the temporal deliverances vouchsafed at various tines to the primitive kingdoms of Israel and Judah were the prototypes, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.5">Isa 25:1-5</reference>. These blessings are described under the figure of a feast made for all nations, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference>; the removing of a veil from their faces, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7">Isa 25:7</reference>; the total extinction of the empire of death by the resurrection from the dead, the exclusion of all sorrow, and the final overthrow of all the enemies of the people of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8-Isa.25.12">Isa 25:8-12</reference>. <div eID="gen27492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27493" type="x-p"/> It does not appear to me that this chapter has any close and particular connection with the chapter immediately preceding, taken separately, and by itself. The subject of that was the desolation of the land of Israel and Judah, by the just judgment of God, for the wickedness and disobedience of the people: which, taken by itself, seems not with any propriety to introduce a hymn of thanksgiving to God for his mercies to his people in delivering them from their enemies. But taking the whole course of prophecies, from the thirteenth to the twenty-fourth chapter inclusive, in which the prophet foretells the destruction of several cities and nations, enemies to the Jews, and of the land of Judah itself, yet with intimations of a remnant to be saved, and a restoration to be at length effected by a glorious establishment of the kingdom of God: with a view to this extensive scene of God's providence in all its parts, and in all its consequences, the prophet may well be supposed to break out into this song of praise; in which his mind seems to be more possessed with the prospect of future mercies than with the recollection of the past. - L. <div eID="gen27493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27494" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27495" type="x-p"/> Thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth - That is, All thy past declarations by the prophets shall be fulfilled in their proper time.
entries.4f50e03839a204fe6ea8deed032a1909b5125040: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27496" type="x-p"/> A city "The city" - Nineveh, Babylon, Ar, Moab, or any other strong fortress possessed by the enemies of the people of God. <div eID="gen27496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27497" type="x-p"/> For the first מעיר meir, of a city, the Syriac and Vulgate read העיר hair, the city; the Septuagint and Chaldee read ערים arim, cities, in the plural, transposing the letters. After the second מעיר meir, a MS. adds לגל lagol, for a heap. <div eID="gen27497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27498" type="x-p"/> A palace of strangers "The palace of the proud ones" - For זרים zarim, strangers, MS. Bodl. and another read זדים zedim, the proud: so likewise the Septuagint; for they render it ασεβων here, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.5">Isa 25:5</reference>, as they do in some other places: see <reference osisRef="Deu.18.20">Deu 18:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.18.22">Deu 18:22</reference>. Another MS. reads צרים tsarim, adversaries; which also makes a good sense. But זרים zarim, strangers, and זדים zedim, the proud, are often confounded by the great similitude of the letters ד daleth and ר resh. See <reference osisRef="Mal.3.15">Mal 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>, in the Septuagint; and <reference osisRef="Psa.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference>, where the Chaldee reads זדים zedim, compared with <reference osisRef="Psa.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference>.
entries.f6b32a9d299f523adbfa5104afee49c5e06c9157: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27499" type="x-p"/> As a storm against the wall "Like a winter-storm" - For קיר kir, read קור kor: or, as עיר ir from ערר arar, so קיר kir from קרר karar. - Capellus.
entries.4e467d87679e48f2ddceabc673595abe464bf8d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27500" type="x-p"/> Of strangers "Of the proud" - The same mistake here as in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa 25:2</reference> (note): see the note there. Here זדים zedim, the proud, is parallel to עריצים aritsim, the formidable: as in <reference osisRef="Psa.54.5">Psa 54:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.86.14">Psa 86:14</reference>. <div eID="gen27500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27501" type="x-p"/> The heat with the shadow of a cloud "As the heat by a thick cloud" - For חרב choreb, the Syriac, Chaldee, Vulgate, and two MSS. read כחרב kechoreb, which is a repetition of the beginning of the foregoing parallel line; and the verse taken out of the parallel form, and more fully expressed, would run thus: "As a thick cloud interposing tempers the heat of the sun on the burnt soil; so shalt thou, by the interposition of thy power, bring low and abate the tumult of the proud, and the triumph of the formidable."
entries.212ebad2f5da439b44d9f5766ccb047061a5eaa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27502" type="x-p"/> In this mountain - Zion, at Jerusalem. In his Church. <div eID="gen27502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27503" type="x-p"/> Shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast - Salvation by Jesus Christ. A feast is a proper and usual expression of joy in consequence of victory, or any other great success. The feast here spoken of is to be celebrated on Mount Sion; and all people, without distinction, are to be invited to it. This can be no other than the celebration of the establishment of Christ's kingdom, which is frequently represented in the Gospel under the image of a feast; "where many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven;" <reference osisRef="Mat.8.11">Mat 8:11</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Luk.14.16">Luk 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.24.29">Luk 24:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.30">Luk 24:30</reference>. This sense is fully confirmed by the concomitants of this feast expressed in the next verse, the removing of the veil from the face of the nations, and the abolition of death: the first of which is obviously and clearly explained of the preaching of the Gospel; and the second must mean the blessing of immortality procured for us by Christ, "who hath abolished death, and through death hath destroyed him that had the power of death." <div eID="gen27503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27504" type="x-p"/> Of wines on the lees "Of old wines" - Hebrews lees; that is, of wines kept long on the lees. The word used to express the lees in the original signifies the preservers; because they preserve the strength and flavor of the wine. "All recent wines, after the fermentation has ceased, ought to be kept on their lees for a certain time, which greatly contributes to increase their strength and flavor. Whenever this first fermentation has been deficient, they will retain a more rich and sweet taste than is natural to them in a recent true vinous state; and unless farther fermentation is promoted by their lying longer on their own lees, they will never attain their genuine strength and flavor, but run into repeated and ineffectual fermentations, and soon degenerate into a liquor of an acetous kind. All wines of a light and austere kind, by a fermentation too great, or too long continued, certainly degenerate into a weak sort of vinegar; while the stronger not only require, but will safely bear a stronger and often-repeated fermentation; and are more apt to degenerate from a defect than excess of fermentation into a vapid, ropy, and at length into a putrescent state." Sir Edward Barry, Observations on the Wines of the Ancients, p. 9, 10. <div eID="gen27504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27505" type="x-p"/> Thevenot observes particularly of the Shiras wine, that, after it is refined from the lees, it is apt to grow sour. "Il a beaucoup de lie; c'est pourquoi il donne puissemment dans la teste; et pour le rendre plus traitable on le passe par un chausse d'hypocras; apres quoi il est fort clair, et moins fumeux. Ils mettent ce vin dans des grandes jarres de terres qui tiennent dix ou douze jusqu'a quatorze carabas: mais quand l'on a entame une jarre, il faut la vuider au plutost, et mettre le vin qu'on en tire dans des bouteilles ou carabas; car si l'on y manque en le laissant quelque tems apres que la jarre est entamee il se gate et s'aigrit." Voyages, Tom. 2 p. 245. "It has much sediment, and therefore is intoxicating. In order to make it more mellow, they strain it through a hypocrates' sleeve, after which it is very clear and less heady. They lay up this wine in great earthen jars, which hold from ten to fourteen carabas: but when a jar is unstopped, it is necessary to empty it immediately, and put the wine into bottles, or carabas; for if it be left thus in the jar, it will spoil and become acid." <div eID="gen27505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27506" type="x-p"/> The caraba, or girba, is a goat's skin drawn off from the animal, having no apertures but those occasioned by the tail, the feet, and the neck. One opening is left, to pour in and draw off the liquor. This skin goes through a sort of tanning process, and is often beautifully ornamented, as is the case with one of these girbas now lying before me. <div eID="gen27506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27507" type="x-p"/> This clearly explains the very elegant comparison, or rather allegory, of Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.11">Jer 48:11</reference>; where the reader will find a remarkable example of the mixture of the proper with the allegorical, not uncommon with the Hebrew poets: - "Moab hath been at ease from his youth, <div eID="gen27507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27508" type="x-p"/> And he hath settled upon his lees; <div eID="gen27508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27509" type="x-p"/> Nor hath he been drawn off from vessel to vessel, <div eID="gen27509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27510" type="x-p"/> Neither hath he gone into captivity: <div eID="gen27510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27511" type="x-p"/> Wherefore his taste remaineth in him, <div eID="gen27511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27512" type="x-p"/> And his flavor is not changed." <div eID="gen27512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27513" type="x-p"/> Sir John Chardin's MS. note on this place of Jeremiah is as follows: "On change ainsi le vin de coupe en coupe en Orient; et quand on en entame une, il faut la vuider en petites coupes ou bouteilles, sans quoy il s'aigrit." "They change the wine from vessel to vessel in the east; and when they unstop a large one, it is necessary to empty it into small vessels, as otherwise it will grow sour."
entries.c352414e4d7d9fb9e201e8c22e9e45d42ae725e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27514" type="x-p"/> The face of the covering cast over all people "The covering that covered the face of all the peoples" - MS. Bodl. reads על פני כל al peney chol. The word פני peney, face, has been removed from its right place into the line above, where it makes no sense; as Houbigant conjectured. "The face of the covering," etc. He will unveil all the Mosaic ritual, and show by his apostles that it referred to, and was accomplished in, the sacrificial offering of Jesus Christ.
entries.0df3bb12800274c573954e074525b886e77b98bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27515" type="x-p"/> He will swallow up death - He, by the grace of God, will taste death for every man. <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">Heb 2:9</reference>. Probably, swallow up death, and taste death, in both these verses, refer to the same thing: Jesus dying instead of a guilty world. These forms of speech may refer to the punishment of certain criminals; they were obliged to drink a cup of poison. That cup which every criminal in the world must have drunk, Jesus Christ drank for them; and thus he swallowed up death: but as he rose again from the dead, complete victory was gained. <div eID="gen27515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27516" type="x-p"/> From these three verses we learn: - <div eID="gen27516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27517" type="x-p"/> I. That the Gospel is a plenteous provision: "I will make a feast for all people." <div eID="gen27517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27518" type="x-p"/> II. That it is a source of light and salvation: "I will destroy the veil. I will abolish death. and bring life and immortality to light." <div eID="gen27518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27519" type="x-p"/> III. That it is a source of comfort and happiness: "I will wipe away all tears from off all faces." <div eID="gen27519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27520" type="x-p"/> As in the Arabic countries a covering was put over the face of him who was condemned to suffer death, it is probable that the words in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7">Isa 25:7</reference> may refer to this. The whole world was condemned to death, and about to be led out to execution, when the gracious Lord interposed, and, by a glorious sacrifice, procured a general pardon.
entries.d8d4dc801af9254ca16b65312b583702b4737d9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27521" type="x-p"/> It shall be said "Shall they say" - So the Septuagint and Vulgate, in the plural number. They read ואמרו veameru, the Syriac reads ואמרת veamarta, thou shalt say. They shall say, i.e., the Jews and the Gentiles - Lo, this [Jesus Christ] is our God: we have waited for him, according to the predictions of the prophets. We have expected him, and we have not been disappointed; therefore will we be glad, and rejoice in his salvation.
entries.3933210d3a62087336b87d5802cd7b7ab8ef4aca: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27522" type="x-p"/> Shall the hand of the Lord rest "The hand of Jehovah shall give rest" - Hebrews תנוח tenuach, quiescet. Annon תניח taniach, quietem dabit, shall rest; shall give rest, ut Graeci, αναπαυσιν δωσει, et Copt.? - Mr. Woide. That is, "shall give peace and quiet to Sion, by destroying the enemy; "as it follows." <div eID="gen27522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27523" type="x-p"/> As straw is trodden down "As the straw is threshed" - Hoc junta ritum loquitur Palastinae et multarum Orientis provinciarum, quae ob pratorum et foeni penuriam paleas preparant esui animantium. Sunt autem carpenta ferrata rotis per medium in serrarum modum se volventibus, quae stipulam conterunt; et comminuunt in paleas. Quomodo igitur plaustris ferratis paleae conteruntur, sic conteretur Moab sub eo; sive sub Dei potentia, sive in semetipso, ut nihil in eo integri remaneat. "This is spoken in reference to the mode of threshing in Palestine, and various other Asiatic provinces. Because of the scarcity of meadow land and hay they make chopped straw for the cattle. They have large wheels studded over with iron teeth or nails, by which, on the out-of-door threshing-floors, they pound and reduce the straw into chaff. As, therefore, the straw is reduced to chaff by bringing the iron-shod wheel over it; so shall Moab be bruised by the power of God, that nothing whole shall remain." - Hieron. in loc. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Isa 28:27</reference> (note). <div eID="gen27523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27524" type="x-p"/> For the dunghill "Under the wheels of the car" - For מדמנה madmenah, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read מרכבה mercabah, which I have followed. See <reference osisRef="Jos.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Jos.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>, where there is a mistake very nearly the same. The keri, במי bemi, is confirmed by twenty-eight MSS., seven ancient, and three editions.
entries.062ce2149a83cad391e90ae5b61e5da93df319e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27525" type="x-p"/> As he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim "As he that sinketh stretcheth out his hands to swim" - There is great obscurity in this place: some understand God as the agent; others, Moab. I have chosen the latter sense, as I cannot conceive that the stretching out of the hands of a swimmer in swimming can be any illustration of the action of God stretching out his hands over Moab to destroy it. I take השחה hashshocheh, altering the point on the ש sin. on the authority of the Septuagint, to be the participle of שחה shachah, the same with שוח shuach, and שחח shachach, to bow down, to be depressed; and that the prophet designed a paronomasia here, a figure which he frequently uses between the similar words שהח shachah, and שחות shechoth. As תחתיו tachtaiv, in his place, or on the spot, as we say in the preceding verse, gives us an idea of the sudden and complete destruction of Moab; so בקרבו bekirbo, in the midst of him, means that this destruction shall be open, and exposed to the view of all: the neighboring nations shall plainly see him struggling against it, as a man in the midst of the deep waters exerts all his efforts by swimming, to save himself from drowning. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.25"/> <div eID="gen27525" type="x-p"/>

entries.429dba41880755d797f9d83117697e2fab09fd4d: <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.5">Isa 25:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen13134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13135" type="x-p"/> The first echo is <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.8">Isa 25:1-8</reference>, or more precisely <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1">Isa 25:1</reference>-5. The prophet, whom we already know as a psalmist from <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1-Isa.12.6">Isa 12:1-6</reference>, now acts as choral leader of the church of the future, and praises Jehovah for having destroyed the mighty imperial city, and proved Himself a defence and shield against its tyranny towards His oppressed church. <hi type="italic">“Jehovah, Thou art my God; I will exalt Thee, I will praise Thy name, that Thou hast wrought wonders, counsels from afar, sincerity, truth. For Thou hast turned it from a city into a heap of stones, the steep castle into a ruin; the palace of the barbarians from being a city, to be rebuilt no more for ever. Therefore a wild people will honour Thee, cities of violent nations fear Thee. For Thou provedst Thyself a stronghold to the lowly, a stronghold to the poor in his distress, as a shelter from the storm of rain, as a shadow from the burning of the sun; for the blast of violent ones was like a storm of rain against a wall. Like the burning of the sun in a parched land, Thou subduest the noise of the barbarians; </hi>(<hi type="italic">like</hi>)<hi type="italic">the burning of the sun through the shadow of a cloud, the triumphal song of violent ones was brought low.”</hi> The introductory clause is to be understood as in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.28">Psa 118:28</reference> : Jehovah (<hi type="italic">voc.</hi>), my God art Thou. “<hi type="italic">Thou hast wrought wonders:</hi>” this is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference> (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.15">Psa 77:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.12">Psa 78:12</reference>; like <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">Isa 12:2</reference>, from <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>). The wonders which are now actually wrought are “<hi type="italic">counsels from afar</hi>” (<hi type="italic">mērâcōk</hi>), counsels already adopted afar off, i.e., long before, thoughts of God belonging to the olden time; the same ideal view as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference> (a parallel which coincides with our passage on every side), and, in fact, throughout the whole of the second part. It is the manifold “counsel” of the Holy One of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.24-Isa.14.27">Isa 14:24-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.12">Isa 19:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">Isa 19:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Isa 23:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Isa 28:29</reference>) which displays its wonders in the events of time. To the verb עשׂית we have also a second and third object, viz., אמן אמוּנה. It is a common custom with Isaiah to place derivatives of the same word side by side, for the purpose of giving the greatest possible emphasis to the idea (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>). אמוּנה indicates a quality, אמן in actual fact. What He has executed is the realization of His faithfulness, and the reality of His promises. The imperial city is destroyed. Jehovah, as the first clause which is defined by <hi type="italic">tzakeph</hi> affirms, has removed it away from the nature of a city into the condition of a heap of stones. The sentence has its object within itself, and merely gives prominence to the change that has been effected; the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> is used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Isa 23:13</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>); the <hi type="italic">min</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference>; Isa 24:10. <hi type="italic">Mappēlâh</hi>, with <hi type="italic">kametz</hi> or <hi type="italic">tzere</hi> before the tone, is a word that can only be accredited from the book of Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Isa 23:13</reference>). עיר, קריה, and אמרון are common parallel words in Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13-Isa.32.14">Isa 32:13-14</reference>); and <hi type="italic">zârim</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7">Isa 1:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">Isa 29:5</reference>, is the most general epithet for the enemies of the people of God. The fall of the imperial kingdom is followed by the conversion of the heathen; the songs proceed from the mouths of the remotest nations. <reference osisRef="Isa.25.3">Isa 25:3</reference> runs parallel with <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Rev 15:3</reference>-4. Nations hitherto rude and passionate now submit to Jehovah with decorous reverence, and those that were previously oppressive (<hi type="italic">‛arı̄tzim</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference>, in form like <hi type="italic">pârı̄tzim</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâlı̄shı̄m</hi>) with humble fear. The cause of this conversion of the heathen is the one thus briefly indicated in the Apocalypse, “for thy judgments are made manifest” (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">Rev 15:4</reference>). דּל and אביון (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.30">Isa 14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">Isa 29:19</reference>) are names well known from the Psalms, as applying to the church when oppressed. To this church, in the distress which she had endured (לו בּצּר, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Isa 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa 63:9</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>), Jehovah had proved Himself a strong castle (<hi type="italic">mâ'ōz</hi>; on the expression, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.30.3">Isa 30:3</reference>), a shelter from storm and a shade from heat (for the figures, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">Isa 16:3</reference>), so that the blast of the tyrants (compare <hi type="italic">ruach</hi> on <reference osisRef="Isa.30.28">Isa 30:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.11">Isa 33:11</reference>, Ps. 76:13) was like a wall-storm, i.e., a storm striking against a wall (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference>, a shoulder-stick, i.e., a stick which strikes the shoulder), sounding against it and bursting upon it without being able to wash it away (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa 28:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.4">Psa 62:4</reference>), because it was the wall of a strong castle, and this strong castle was Jehovah Himself. As Jehovah can suddenly subdue the heat of the sun in dryness (<hi type="italic">tzâyōn</hi>, abstract for concrete, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>, equivalent to dry land, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">Isa 41:18</reference>), and it must give way when He brings up a shady thicket (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">Jer 4:29</reference>), namely of clouds (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.9">Exo 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>), so did He suddenly subdue the thundering (<hi type="italic">shâ'on</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Isa 17:12</reference>) of the hordes that stormed against His people; and the song of triumph (<hi type="italic">zâmı̄r</hi>, only met with again in Sol 2:12) of the tyrants, which passed over the world like a scorching heat, was soon “brought low” (<hi type="italic">‛ânâh</hi>, in its neuter radical signification “to bend,” related to כּנע, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Isa 31:4</reference>).
entries.542d61bd47aafccd708958b11d82f36207d24892: <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference> <div eID="gen13135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13136" type="x-p"/> Thus the first hymnic echo dies away; and the eschatological prophecy, coming back to <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference>, but with deeper prayerlike penetration, proceeds thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah of hosts prepares for all nations upon this mountain a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things rich in marrow, of wines on the lees thoroughly strained.”</hi> “<hi type="italic">This mountain</hi>” is Zion, the seat of God’s presence, and the place of His church’s worship. The feast is therefore a spiritual one. The figure is taken, as in Psa 22:27., from the sacrificial meals connected with the <hi type="italic">shelâmim</hi> (the peace-offerings). <hi type="italic">Shemârim</hi> <hi type="italic">mezukkâkim</hi> are wines which have been left to stand upon their lees after the first fermentation is over, which have thus thoroughly fermented, and have been kept a long time (from <hi type="italic">shâmar</hi>, to keep, <hi type="italic">spec</hi>. to allow to ferment), and which are then filtered before drinking (Gr. οἶνος σακκίας, i.e., διΰλισμένος or διηθικὸς, from διηθεῖν, <hi type="italic">percolare</hi>), hence wine both strong and clear. <hi type="italic">Memuchâyı̄m</hi> might mean <hi type="italic">emedullatae</hi> (“with the marrow taken out;” compare, perhaps, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.3">Pro 31:3</reference>), but this could only apply to the bones, not to the fat meat itself; the meaning is therefore “mixed with marrow,” made marrowy, <hi type="italic">medullosae</hi>. The thing symbolized in this way is the full enjoyment of blessedness in the perfected kingdom of God. The heathen are not only humbled so that they submit to Jehovah, but they also take part in the blessedness of His church, and are abundantly satisfied with the good things of His house, and made to drink of pleasure as from a river (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>). The ring of the v. is inimitably pictorial. It is like joyful music to the heavenly feast. The more flexible form ממחיים (from the original, ממחי = ממחה) is intentionally chosen in the place of ממּסהים. It is as if we heard stringed instruments played with the most rapid movement of the bow.
entries.b0b43338ebaa2287383cc845b1ab5d7518afb9d4: <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7-Isa.25.8">Isa 25:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13137" type="x-p"/> Although the feast is one earth, it is on an earth which has been transformed into heaven; for the party-wall between God and the world has fallen down: death is no more, and all tears are for ever wiped away. <hi type="italic">“And He casts away upon this mountain the veil that veiled over all peoples, and the covering that covered over all nations. He puts away death for ever; and the Lord Jehovah wipes the tear from every face; and He removes the shame of His people from the whole earth: for Jehovah hath spoken it.”</hi> What Jehovah bestows is followed by what He puts away. The “veil” and “covering” (<hi type="italic">massēcâh</hi>, from <hi type="italic">nâsac</hi> = <hi type="italic">mâsâc</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8">Isa 22:8</reference>, from <hi type="italic">sâcac</hi>, to weave, twist, and twist over = to cover) are not symbols of mourning and affliction, but of spiritual blindness, like the “veil” upon the heart of Israel mentioned in 2Co 3:15. The <hi type="italic">penē hallōt</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Job.41.5">Job 41:5</reference>) is the upper side of the veil, the side turned towards you, by which Jehovah takes hold of the veil to lift it up. The second <hi type="italic">hallōt</hi> stands for הלּט (Ges. §71, Anm. 1), and is written in this form, according to Isaiah’s peculiar style (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.11">Isa 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Isa 22:13</reference>), merely for the sake of the sound, like the obscurer <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> forms in Isa 24:3. The only difference between the two nouns is this: in <hi type="italic">lōt</hi> the leading idea is that of the completeness of the covering, and in <hi type="italic">massēcâh</hi> that of its thickness. The removing of the veil, as well as of death, is called בּלּע, which we find applied to God in other passages, viz., <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Isa 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.21.10">Psa 21:10</reference>; Psa 55:10. Swallowing up is used elsewhere as equivalent to making a thing disappear, by taking it into one’s self; but here, as in many other instances, the notion of receiving into one’s self is dropped, and nothing remains but the idea of taking away, unless, indeed, abolishing of death may perhaps be regarded as taking it back into what hell shows to be the <hi type="italic">eternal</hi> principle of wrath out of which God called it forth. God will abolish death, so that there shall be no trace left of its former sway. Paul gives a free rendering of this passage in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">1Co 15:54</reference>, κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος (after the Aramaean <hi type="italic">netzach</hi>, <hi type="italic">vincere</hi>). The Syriac combines both ideas, that of the Targum and that of Paul: <hi type="italic">absorpta est mors per victoriam in sempiternum</hi>. But the abolition of death is not in itself the perfection of blessedness. There are sufferings which force out a sigh, even after death has come as a deliverance. But all these sufferings, whose ultimate ground is sin, Jehovah sweeps away. There is something very significant in the use of the expression דּמעה (a tear), which the Apocalypse renders πᾶν δάκρυον (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.4">Rev 21:4</reference>). Wherever there is a tear on any face whatever, Jehovah wipes it away; and if Jehovah wipes away, this must be done most thoroughly: He removes the cause with the outward symptom, the sin as well as the tear. It is self-evident that this applies to the church triumphant. The world has been judged, and what was salvable has been saved. There is therefore no more shame for the people of God. Over the whole earth there is no further place to be found for this; Jehovah has taken it away. The earth is therefore a holy dwelling-place for blessed men. The new Jerusalem is Jehovah’s throne, but the whole earth is Jehovah’s glorious kingdom. The prophet is here looking from just the same point of view as Paul in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.28">1Co 15:28</reference>, and John in the last page of the Apocalypse.
entries.102263f5a1a7210fc7e73f839312a284dba4e5f3: <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">Isa 25:9</reference> <div eID="gen13137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13138" type="x-p"/> After this prophetic section, which follows the first melodious echo like an interpolated recitative, the song of praise begins again; but it is soon deflected into the tone of prophecy. The shame of the people of God, mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Isa 25:8</reference>, recals to mind the special enemies of the church in its immediate neighbourhood, who could not tyrannize over it indeed, like the empire of the world, but who nevertheless scoffed at it and persecuted it. The representative and emblem of these foes are the proud and boasting Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29">Jer 48:29</reference>). All such attempts as that of Knobel to turn this into history are but so much lost trouble. Moab is a mystic name. It is the prediction of the humiliation of Moab in this spiritual sense, for which the second echo opens the way by celebrating Jehovah’s appearing. Jehovah is now in His manifested presence the conqueror of death, the drier of tears, the saviour of the honour of His oppressed church. <hi type="italic">“And they say in that day, Behold our God, for whom we waited to help us: this is Jehovah, for whom we waited; let us be glad and rejoice in His salvation.”</hi> The undefined but self-evident subject to <hi type="italic">v'âmar</hi> (“they say”) is the church of the last days. “Behold:” <hi type="italic">hinnēh</hi> and <hi type="italic">zeh</hi> belong to one another, as in Isa 21:9. The <hi type="italic">waiting</hi> may be understood as implying a retrospective glance at all the remote past, even as far back as Jacob’s saying, “I wait for Thy salvation, O Jehovah” (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.18">Gen 49:18</reference>). The appeal, “Let us be glad,” etc., has passed over into the grand <hi type="italic">hodu</hi> of Psa 118:24.
entries.f1b21e05147793d9721982d35e8a216f300eecff: <reference osisRef="Isa.25.10-Isa.25.12">Isa 25:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen13138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13139" type="x-p"/> In the land of promise there is rejoicing, but on the other side of the Jordan there is fear of ruin. Two contrasted pictures are placed here side by side. The Jordan is the same as the “great gulf” in the parable of the rich man. Upon Zion Jehovah descends in mercy, but upon the highlands of Moab in His wrath. <hi type="italic">“For the hand of Jehovah will sink down upon this mountain, and Moab is trodden down there where it is, as straw is trodden down in the water of the dung-pit. And he spreadeth out his hands in the pool therein, as the swimmer spreadeth them out to swim; but Jehovah forceth down the pride of Moab in spite of the artifices of his hands. Yea, thy steep, towering walls He bows down, forces under, and casts earthwards into dust.”</hi> Jehovah brings down His hand upon Zion (<hi type="italic">nūach</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.2">Isa 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>), not only to shelter, but also to avenge. Israel, that has been despised, He now makes glorious, and for contemptuous Moab He prepares a shameful end. In the place where it now is תּחתּיו, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.10">2Sa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.16">Hab 3:16</reference>, “in its own place,” its own land) it is threshed down, stamped or trodden down, as straw is trodden down into a dung-pit to turn it into manure: <hi type="italic">hiddūsh</hi>, the <hi type="italic">inf. constr.</hi>, with the vowel sound <hi type="italic">u</hi>, possibly to distinguish it from the <hi type="italic">inf. absol.</hi> <hi type="italic">hiddosh</hi> (Ewald, §240,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). Instead of בּמו (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa 43:2</reference>), the <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> has בּמי (cf., <reference osisRef="Job.9.30">Job 9:30</reference>); and this is probably the more correct reading, since <hi type="italic">madmēnâh</hi>, by itself, means the dunghill, and not the tank of dung water. At the same time, it is quite possible that <hi type="italic">b'mo</hi> is intended as a play upon the name <hi type="italic">Moab</hi>, just as the word <hi type="italic">madmēnâh</hi> may possibly have been chosen with a play upon the Moabitish <hi type="italic">Madmēn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>).
